newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court upholds USDA generic ad program.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court upholds USDA generic ad program.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court Wednesday upheld a federal programme that requires California fruit growers to chip in for industrywide, generic advertising campaigns, saying it was not a violation of free speech rights.
The High Court, by a 5-4 vote, reversed an appeals court ruling that the assessments were unconstitutional.
Justice John Paul Stevens said for the court majority that the requirement that respondents finance generic advertising does not violate the First Amendment.

For the dissenting judges, Justice David Souter wrote: "...forced payment for commercial speech should be subject to the same level of judicial scrutiny as a restriction on communications in that category. Because I believe that the advertising scheme here fails that test, I respectfully dissent."

Under an agricultural marketing law from the New Deal era, producers and distributors of California peaches, plums and nectarines are required to pool advertising dollars. A group of growers had challenged the marketing requirement, claiming a First Amendment right not to engage in government-compelled speech.

The Agriculture Department defended the programme, saying the fees were like union dues and that the advertising boosted sales. It also argued that mandatory assessments were necessary to prevent growers from getting a "free ride" from commercials funded by other growers.
